https://www.dw.com/en/russia-bridge-buil.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5IAWj A satellite image of bridge construction between Russia and North Korea from late June. Clearly visible at the top right: the large processing facilities on the Russian side. Image: Planet Labs Advertisement For years, Khasan was little more than a very remote place on the edge of Russia . Less than 500 people live in the village in the country's far east, more than 5,600 miles (9,012 kilometers) from Moscow. But it's here that Russia shares a mere 10.5-mile border with North Korea — and Khasan is the only Russian settlement along that short stretch. Since 1959, the so-called Korean-Russian Friendship Railway Bridge has crossed the Tumen River here, serving as the only land connection between the two countries. But in recent years, Russia and North Korea have been building a parallel road bridge just a few hundred yards away. The bridge is now nearing completion ahead of schedule, raising concerns in Kyiv that Russia could use it to secretly bring North Korean troops to the front lines in Ukraine . Since the start of Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Moscow and Pyongyang have improved their ties . Both countries face Western sanctions and are diplomatically largely isolated. In June 2024, Russian President Vladimir Putin and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un signed a strategic partnership deal which in part focused on expanding military cooperation. That meant large-scale weapons shipments as well as the deployment of North Korean soldiers to support Russia's war in Ukraine. At the same time, both governments agreed to build the new road bridge. "The opening of the new bridge will boost bilateral trade, optimize logistics, strengthen cultural ties and transform border regions into dynamically growing economic centers," Russian Transport Minister Andrey Nikitin said at the time. Not particularly attractive to tourists: until now, the only crossing over the border river was an old, single-lane "Railway Bridge of Friendship." Image: Yuri Smityuk/TASS/picture alliance The Washington-based Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) has also pointed to the bridge's economic significance, noting that "the pace at which construction of the road bridge is progressing, and the continued high level of rail traffic at previously dormant rail yards, are clear indicators of the importance and expansion of trade between the two countries during Russia's ongoing war against Ukraine." A project for trade and tourism? But according to British newspaper The Guardian , there are major doubts that civilian economic goals are the project's true primary purpose. Official data shows that trade between Russia and North Korea amounted to just $34 million in 2024. The bridge and its immediate infrastructure are thought to cost roughly $100 million. Satellite pictures of the site show warehouses, customs facilities, truck areas and a helicopter pad being built. Cultivating a "strategic partnership": North Korean leader Kim Jong Un and Russian President Vladimir Putin. Image: Sergey Bobylev/Sputnik/REUTERS Ukrainian human rights organization Truth Hounds, which has been monitoring the project , also doubts the bridge is for tourism. It is about 125 hours by car from Moscow and about four hours from Vladivostok. "Tourism in North Korea is heavily restricted and, given the country's isolation, cannot expand rapidly," the organization said. If anyone from Russia would visit North Korea, they probably would go to the capital, Pyongyang, rather than the country's remote northeastern region. But Pyongyang is hundreds of miles from the border, and "few people would want to make that journey by car," the group argued. Russia has spent years trying to get tourists to take heavily subsidized flights to visit Pyongyang. However, not many have taken up the opportunity. In 2025, fewer than 10,000 Russian citizens are thought to have traveled to North Korea. Here, the boss makes the beds himself: Kim Jong Un inspects a tourist hotel. But demand from Russians for holidays in North Korea is rather low. Image: YONHAP NEWS AGENCY/picture alliance Or a cover for military transport? Truth Hounds instead concludes that the bridge's real purpose is to deepen military cooperation, particularly by facilitating the transfer of North Korean troops and weapons for the war in Ukraine. According to unofficial information reported by South Korean, Ukrainian and US sources in the middle of last year, North Korea sent between 14,000 and 15,000 personnel to support Russia's war, with many reportedly deployed in Russia's Kursk region while parts of it were under Ukrainian control. North Korea has also supplied Russia with weapons. Road transport, Truth Hounds suggests, is harder to monitor by satellite than rail transport. Trains are confined to fixed tracks, and loading and unloading can take place only at designated rail hubs. Trucks however, can load and unload almost anywhere and satellite surveillance is virtually impossible. Ukrainian sources published this image in October 2024. It reportedly shows North Korean soldiers being issued Russian uniforms at a Siberian military training ground. Image: Ukraine Photo/Newscom/picture alliance Just days ago, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned on X that Russia could deploy as many as 30,000 additional North Korean troops in the war against Ukraine. Military know-how for North Korea Zelenskyy also argued that North Korean leader Kim Jong Un from the improved military partnership. The new bridge could enable Russia to secretly move resources into North Korea. "Russia," Zelenskyy wrote, "is helping North Korea learn how to wage modern war, improve its weapons and gain real combat experience in using them." Observers also believe that North Korea might be receiving some Russian nuclear technology in exchange for helping Moscow in its war efforts. Taken together, Zelenskyy warned in his X post, these developments pose "a threat to everyone in Asia who lives within range of North Korean missiles." This article has been translated from German. https://economictimes.indiatimes.com/new.text: Vilnius [Lithuania]: European Union foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas asserted that Europe must secure reciprocal advantages in any upcoming settlement addressing the Russia-Ukraine conflict, emphasising that any viable peace architecture will require substantial commitments from European partners.Kallas delivered the comments during an official visit to Lithuania on Monday (local time), following diplomatic missions undertaken over the weekend by United States negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner to Moscow and Kyiv in an effort to jump-start peace initiatives.Speaking at a joint press briefing alongside Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevicius, Kallas addressed inquiries regarding whether the weekend discussions had advanced peace prospects and the implications of a potential trilateral summit excluding an EU representative.She underscored that direct dialogue between Moscow and Kyiv remains essential. On the European side, it is clear that we cannot be mediators between Russia and Ukraine. They need to talk to each other. We have always been on the side of Ukraine, so we are not neutral in this situation, Kallas stated.The EU foreign policy chief further noted that any prospective accord would entail extensive demands placed upon Europe, stressing that such contributions must be matched with tangible benefits.She said that any eventual peace agreement would also involve a lot of asks for Europe, adding that these were not things Europe should give without getting anything in return. On Monday, Kallas held discussions with Lithuanian President Gitanas Nauseda, focusing on the strategic objectives outlined for Lithuania's forthcoming presidency of the Council of the European Union, Xinhua news agency reported.President Nauseda outlined that the Lithuanian presidency would prioritise continental security and defence matters, European integration, market competitiveness, domestic safety, and societal resilience.Parallel diplomatic tracks saw Russian President Vladimir Putin receive US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner for talks at the Kremlin on Saturday, which extended past three hours.Subsequently, Witkoff and Kushner travelled to Kyiv to meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Sunday.Prior diplomatic engagements involved delegations from Ukraine, the United States, and Russia convening for two rounds of discussions in Abu Dhabi on January 23-24 and February 4-5, followed by a subsequent round in Geneva on February 17-18, aimed at exploring pathways to resolve the ongoing conflict.These trilateral negotiations have since stalled and remain suspended.

Israel’s foreign minister described the tiny Pacific island nation of some 12,000 people as “one of Israel’s greatest friends in the international community.” Two days later, it was Slovenia’s turn, as Saar cut the ribbon on a new embassy in Ljubljana. He praised the new center-right government for standing by Israel in the European Union, especially after the country had previously been one of Israel’s harshest critics. A large business delegation was brought along to show appreciation. There was no such celebration in London, where Israel faced one of its sharpest diplomatic rebukes in years: a coordinated move by the United Kingdom and 11 other countries to impose sanctions and trade restrictions on Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank. Israel has had no ambassador in London for nearly a year. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s intended envoy, his chief of staff Tzachi Braverman, was barred from leaving Israel due to a criminal investigation, leaving the post vacant. The split-screen moment reflects a broader pattern in Israel’s foreign relations: As traditional partners in Western Europe grow distant, losing patience with the settlement expansion and surging violence in the West Bank, the right-wing government is cultivating ties with smaller or what it sees as more ideologically aligned countries, redirecting its diplomatic energy to other arenas. UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband tied the new measures, announced in parliament on Tuesday, directly to Israel’s decision to push ahead with the E1 settlement project, which critics say would cut the West Bank in two and close off the possibility of a contiguous future Palestinian state. But the move is part of a longer-term shift. In September 2025, Britain, Canada, France and more than a dozen other Western states recognized Palestinian statehood. And this June, the UK, Canada, France, Norway, Australia and New Zealand announced a wave of coordinated sanctions targeting individuals and networks accused of financing and enabling settler violence. Some of the states announced additional punitive measures: France barred far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich from entering the country, Italy opened an investigation into National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir over the treatment of detained activists, including Italians, after Israel intercepted an aid flotilla on its way to Gaza. The Netherlands declared both Ben Gvir and Smotrich “persona non grata” and approved its own ban on imports of settlement goods. Not every proposal has succeeded, and Israel has so far managed to stall broader actions from the EU. For years, Israel used Viktor Orban’s government in Hungary to block EU measures. Now, following a change in leadership in Budapest, Slovenia has effectively taken Hungary’s place as Israel’s representative in Brussels. A push by France and Sweden for an EU ban on settlement trade was stalled, as were efforts to expel Israel from the EU’s flagship Horizon research program. Dr. Rémi Daniel, from Israel’s Institute for National Security Studies (INSS) says the one comfort for Israel is that Germany and Italy have so far stuck to statements rather than joining the sanctions. “They are the most important EU member states because they have the power to block plans at the European level,” he said. But the trend was still concerning, he said, because looking at the balance of power within the EU, “the swinging center is going more against Israel.” Even as ties with some Western European allies fray, others are deepening their alliance with Israel through defense trade. Last month, Israel signed a $3.5 billion air-defense deal with Greece, one of the largest arm agreements in Israel’s history. And in early 2026, Israel Aerospace Industries signed a $3.1 billion deal with Germany to expand its supply of Arrow missile interceptor systems. Israel’s response to the new sanctions – and its attitude towards one of its oldest allies in general – has been openly combative. Saar swiftly announced he would close the British Consulate General in Jerusalem, end UK training for Palestinian Authority security forces, and ban entry to a dozen British officials and lawmakers. “The British move is morally distorted and constitutes a blatant interference in the affairs of a sovereign state and its electoral process,” Saar said Tuesday. Netanyahu labeled the UK the “Islamic Republic of Britain” on a podcast last month and has accused French President Emanuel Macron of fueling antisemitism by recognizing a Palestinian state. While relations with some Western allies cool, and even the friendly Trump administration in the United States appears to be growingly frustrated with settler violence, Israel has been pouring energies into other regions and redrawing its map of relationships. Declaring 2026 “The Year of South America,” Saar has toured Argentina, Ecuador, Paraguay and Colombia and restored relations with Bolivia, Chile and Honduras. He also opened a communication channel with Venezuela for the first time since 2009, sending rescue teams to assist with earthquake relief last month. New Israeli embassies opened in Zambia, Estonia, Moldova, Fiji and Slovenia. And Israel became the first country in the world to recognize the self-declared Republic of Somaliland as an independent state. Somaliland then opened an embassy in Jerusalem, where fewer than 10 countries have embassies, including the US. Argentina, Colombia, Costa Rica and the Democratic Republic of Congo have declared their intent to join the list. Daniel Shek, a former Israeli ambassador to France, argues that this pivot comes at a real cost and says the government is damaging relationships built over decades on shared interests in economy, science, culture, security. “They are sacrificing the alliances with the most significant countries,” he said. “If Saar thinks the Paraguayan economy can replace France as a partner for export and import, good for him.” The countries involved in the sanctions, he said, are not ideologically hostile to Israel, just its actions under Netanyahu, Ben Gvir and Smotrich. “France, Britain, Italy, the Netherlands, are friendly countries fed up with this Israeli government’s behavior.” Shek notes that the sanctions target the settlements, and not Israel itself, and that their practical bite, for now, is limited. Still, he says, they should not be underestimated. “Once sanctions have been imposed, it is significant,” he said. “There are things that have been opened and cannot be put back in the bottle.” The-CNN-Wire ™ & © 2026 Cable News Network, Inc., a Warner Bros.
